newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS-Home builder Lennar acquiring Pacific Greystone.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Home builder Lennar acquiring Pacific Greystone.

text.p: Leading Florida home builder Lennar Corp. expanded westward Wednesday with a $521 million stock-swap acquisition of homebuilder Pacific Greystone Corp. of California.

The deal was expected to close by year's end and would give Lennar a commanding spot among home builders in Texas, Arizona, Nevada and California, the biggest U.S. new housing market just coming out of a long slump in home building.
Lennar is already the biggest home builder in Florida, and a combined Lennar-Greystone would be the fifth largest builder of single-family homes in the United States.

Lennar also announced it was spinning off to shareholders its fast-growing finance unit, a mix of commercial real estate businesses and mortgage-related securities investments bought cheaply during the savings-and-loan and real-estate crises of the early 1990s.

Industry analysts and executives said Wall Street had long undervalued Lennar's finance unit and that the spinoff would allow the company to borrow more heavily and at lower rates. Lennar Chief Executive Stuart Miller said the spinoff, LPC Inc., would be able to add as much as $2 billion in debt.

Closley held Lennar, based in Miami, said it will hold 68 percent of the company after the merger with Greystone, owner of dozens of residential projects in northern and southern California, including Orange County. Lennar is also securing a top spot in Houston.
"This deal puts them three or four years up the product curve in California," said analyst Timothy Jones of Southeast Research Partners.

One industry executive said the combined company would have nearly 14,000 home sites in California and a substantial infrastructure for building homes. The company would also have cost and bargaining advantages with banks, land sellers and subcontractors who build individual homes.
Miller, who will be chairman of LPC as well as chief executive of Lennar, said a key goal of the moves was to narrow the company's exposure to any single regional housing market.
"Business cycles need to be defined regionally, and even locally," he said. "I don't believe we are at the top of a cycle in California. We are in a comfort zone."

Each share of Greystone will be exchanged for 1.138 shares in the new company. With 14.96 million shares outstanding, the transaction values Greystone at about $521 million, based on Wednesday's closing price for Lennar.
Both deals are contingent on the spinoff winning tax-free status from the U.S. government. Lennar executives said they were highly confident such a ruling would come.
Stock in Greystone, which was based in Los Angeles, lost $2 and closed at $15.125, while Lennar closed up $4.25 at $30.625, in consolidated trading on the New York Stock Exchange.
Lennar is controlled by its founder and chairman, Leonard Miller, who, through ownership of a Class B series of stock, holds 79 percent of the voting shares.
